summary: Iran and the US trade claims over Hormuz as Trump says the war will end soon, AI spending fears hit Big Tech, a record crypto theft, Ebola deaths pass 5,000 and Israel's vote ends in deadlock.

topics.heading: Iran reports more tanker fires in Hormuz as Trump says the war will 'wrap up soon'
topics.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say two more tankers were stopped after 'incidents' in the Strait of Hormuz, while the US military says the main shipping lanes are clear of mines. Qatar is waiting for Iran's answer to a new peace draft.[^1][^3]

lead.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guard reports two tankers on fire in Strait of Hormuz as talks continue

alsoReported.title: Trump says Iran war will end soon, US military insists Hormuz is secure
Tankers strike mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says, as Hegseth fires top general

article: On Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said two more tankers had "incidents" in the Strait of Hormuz and were stopped, claiming the ships had switched off their tracking systems and had US military support[^1]. A day earlier the IRGC said three tankers hit mines, and Iran's regular military later put the number at four[^2]. Independent confirmation is thinner. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO), which tracks shipping incidents, reported a small boat attaching two explosive devices to a tanker's hull off Khasab, Oman; the ship was briefly disabled, the crew was safe and it sailed on[^1]. Oman's navy also rescued 25 crew from a burning ship near Musandam[^1].

The US military tells a different story. Adm. Brad Cooper, who leads US Central Command (CENTCOM), says the main shipping lanes are clear of mines, and CENTCOM rejected IRGC claims that it had captured a US drone[^1][^3]. President Trump said on a radio show that the war is "going to get wrapped up soon," adding that the US needs a guarantee that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon[^1][^3].

Background: the war began in February, and Iran has tightly limited traffic through the strait, a narrow channel that carries a large share of the world's oil[^1]. Diplomacy runs alongside the fighting. Qatar gave Iran a draft on October 25 with a seven-day schedule of confidence-building steps; a senior Iranian official called it "unacceptable ideas and not an offer," but Qatari mediators were back in Tehran on Friday, and a reply was expected around the weekend[^2][^4].

What next is unclear. The Wall Street Journal reports that the US told Gulf states to prepare for a "short, intense" campaign after the November 3 US midterm elections, while AP, citing two diplomats, says no final decision has been made[^2]. My read: as long as ships are attacked, fuel costs stay high far from the Gulf, and the next few days, with Iran's reply to Qatar and the US vote, may show which way this goes.
topics.differences: Iran says several tankers hit mines or were stopped; UKMTO has confirmed one explosive attack, and the US says the main lanes are clear[^1][^3]. On a letter from US Vice-President JD Vance to Iran, the Wall Street Journal reports it set out a negotiating framework, while Trump said it was about medical supplies[^2].

topics.heading: Alphabet's record one-day drop leads a Big Tech slide over the cost of AI
topics.summary: Alphabet shares fell 12.6% on Thursday, their worst day since 2004, after heavy AI spending and slower search growth. By Friday's close the Nasdaq had lost about 5% in October, its worst month since March 2025.[^5][^6]

lead.title: Alphabet's worst day ever leaves Google search valued below fossil fuel stocks, BofA says

alsoReported.title: Stock market today: Nasdaq, Dow, S&P 500 clobbered as October closes with brutal sell-off
Nasdaq Faces $2 Trillion Wipeout in October as AI Spending Fears Deepen

article: Shares of Alphabet, Google's parent company, fell 12.6% on Thursday, their worst day since the stock began trading in 2004, wiping out about $482 billion in market value[^5]. Investors focused on two things: search revenue grew 12%, slower than the 15% analysts expected, and the company spent $51.4 billion on capital projects, mostly AI data centres, in a single quarter, leaving it with negative free cash flow[^5]. Free cash flow is the cash left after a company pays for its investments.

Other results added to the worry. Intel forecast lower sales than expected, saying a shortage of memory chips is pushing up PC prices, and its shares fell more than 20% after hours[^6][^17]. Amazon's profit per share missed estimates even as its cloud business grew 39%[^6]. Meta's shares are more than 20% below their high after it announced a record $97.5 billion fundraising[^6][^7]. On Friday the Nasdaq fell 2.86% and the S&P 500 1.82%; Reuters says more than $2 trillion was erased from the Nasdaq 100 in October[^6][^7].

Background: the largest tech companies are borrowing and spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build AI. Alphabet alone plans about $200 billion of such spending this year and $300 billion in 2027[^5]. Parts of the business are booming: Google Cloud's revenue roughly doubled[^5]. The question investors are asking is when all that spending will pay for itself.

My read: these companies are so large that their swings move pension funds and ordinary savings, so the AI spending question reaches far beyond Silicon Valley. One bad month does not mean the boom is over, but it shows that investors' patience has limits, especially while interest rates are rising.

topics.heading: Hackers steal about $6.3 billion from Binance, the largest crypto theft on record
topics.summary: Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, says hackers took about $6.3 billion in roughly 20 minutes. Blockchain analysts link the attack to a North Korean hacking unit; about $3 billion has been frozen.[^8]

lead.title: Binance says $6.3bn stolen in biggest crypto heist in history: What we know

alsoReported.title: Stock market today: Nasdaq, Dow, S&P 500 clobbered as October closes with brutal sell-off

article: Binance says hackers stole about $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency, mostly within about 20 minutes, across ten different blockchains, starting late on Thursday[^8]. That is roughly four times the previous record, the $1.5 billion taken from the exchange Bybit in February 2025[^8]. Binance suspended withdrawals, promised to cover all customer losses, and said it expected to reopen withdrawals within about 45 hours[^8].

About $3 billion has been frozen so far, including more than $2.3 billion by Tether and Circle, companies that issue "stablecoins", digital tokens tied to the US dollar that their issuers can lock[^8]. The blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean unit linked to the Lazarus Group[^8]. North Korea usually denies involvement in such attacks[^8].

Background: crypto theft has become a major source of money for North Korea, which is under heavy international sanctions, and it helps fund the country's weapons programmes[^8]. The theft added to Friday's market slide, and Bitcoin fell to a six-week low of about $76,400[^8][^6].

Why it matters: if the attribution holds, this is one of the largest thefts ever linked to a state, and it tests whether exchanges and regulators can trace and recover stolen money. My read: the fact that so much was frozen shows crypto is less anonymous than many people think, but the rest may be hard to recover. It is also a reminder that money held on an exchange is only as safe as the company running it.

topics.heading: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 5,000 deaths, the second-deadliest on record
topics.summary: Congo's health ministry reports 5,026 Ebola deaths among more than 10,000 cases, with cases also in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. The strain involved has no approved vaccine or treatment.[^9][^10]

lead.title: Congo's Ebola deaths top 5,000 as fear of continent-wide spread mounts

alsoReported.title: Ebola cases in DR Congo surpass 10,000 in fastest-growing outbreak

article: Congo's health ministry says the Ebola outbreak there has now killed 5,026 people out of 10,351 recorded cases, while 2,788 people have recovered[^9]. That makes it the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, after the 2014-16 epidemic in West Africa, which killed about 11,000 people[^9]. The disease has reached 67 of Congo's 178 health zones, in eight provinces[^9].

It has also crossed borders. Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria have reported cases; Kenya has had eight cases and two deaths, and Nigeria's one patient was evacuated to Switzerland[^9]. Dr. Patrick Otim of the World Health Organization called the milestone "very tragic," stressing that each death is more than a number[^9].

Background: the outbreak was declared on May 15 and is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, which has killed nearly half of the people it has infected here[^9]. The existing Ebola vaccines were made for a different strain, Zaire, so there is no approved vaccine or treatment for this one; a first vaccine trial began in late October[^9][^10].

Why it matters: AP reports that about 80% of new cases are outside known contact chains, meaning they are not linked to people health workers were already watching, and that about a third of deaths happen before patients reach care[^9]. Both are signs the virus is spreading faster than it can be tracked. My read: the things to watch are early results from the vaccine trial and whether neighbouring countries can keep their case numbers low.

topics.heading: Evacuation begins from occupied Oleshky under a rare local truce in Ukraine
topics.summary: A US-brokered local ceasefire let aid in and civilians out of Russian-occupied Oleshky, while strikes elsewhere killed at least 27 civilians on Oct 29. The truce is due to end on Sunday, November 1.[^11][^12][^13]

lead.title: Oleshky evacuation begins but volunteer claims Russia already moved people outside of agreed terms

alsoReported.title: Russia and Ukraine say aid operation and evacuations underway in Russian-controlled Oleshky
Russian ballistic missiles kill a man in Kyiv, capping a day that left at least 27 civilians dead across Ukraine

article: On Friday, buses and aid convoys began moving in and out of Oleshky, a town in the Russian-occupied part of Ukraine's Kherson region, under a local ceasefire brokered by the United States[^11][^12]. About 2,000 people still live there, down from about 24,000 before the war[^12]. Some evacuees went to Russian-held areas and some to Ukrainian-held territory, by a route through Belarus[^12]. Ukraine's human-rights ombudsman said the truce had held for 80 hours[^11].

The operation was not smooth. A Ukrainian volunteer and an anonymous source told the Kyiv Independent that Russia began moving people a day early and threatened residents with "filtration", a screening process run by Russian authorities[^11]. There is no confirmed count of how many people left[^11][^12].

Away from Oleshky, the war went on. On October 29, Russian strikes killed at least 27 civilians across six regions, according to a tally of regional officials' reports by Euromaidan Press, including the drone strike on a railway platform in Dnipro[^13]. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched ballistic missiles and 113 drones that day[^13].

What next: the truce is due to end on Sunday evening, November 1[^12]. Talks between US, Ukrainian and Russian teams are expected to resume next month in Abu Dhabi, the first such round since February[^12]. My read: small local deals like this one test whether the two sides can trust each other at all, but they are a long way from a general ceasefire, and the two still disagree on territory.
topics.differences: Accounts of the evacuation's start differ: a Ukrainian volunteer says Russia moved people early and outside the agreed terms[^11]. Death tolls for the Dnipro strike also vary slightly, with regional authorities giving 15 and some outlets at least 14[^13].

topics.heading: Israel's final results leave neither bloc with a majority; officials reject fraud claims
topics.summary: Final results give Netanyahu's bloc 53 of 120 seats, the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot 48 and Arab-led parties a record 19. The election committee says there is no basis for Likud's claim that the vote was stolen.[^14][^15]

lead.title: How can Israel break its election deadlock?

alsoReported.title: Israel final election results: Netanyahu's bloc maintains lead but does not secure majority

article: Israel's Central Elections Committee has published final results from the October 27 vote. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats, the bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot won 48, and Arab-led parties won 19, their best result ever[^14][^15]. A government needs 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats, so no side has a majority[^14]. Netanyahu's Likud is still the largest single party, with 27 seats[^16].

Likud says the Arab-led parties "stole" the election, but it has not published proof[^14]. The committee's acting director general, Dean Livne, said there was "no basis" for claims of election theft, and police say they will look into any credible complaint[^15].

There are a few possible paths. On the opposition side, the Arab-led party Ra'am is reported to be open to joining an Eisenkot government, and the Joint List might support a minority government from outside it[^14]. But Avigdor Lieberman, whose party is in the opposition bloc, has objected to relying on Arab parties, and Netanyahu may push for yet another election[^14].

What next: official results go to President Isaac Herzog on November 4, and the new Knesset is sworn in on November 10[^16]. Why it matters: the next government will shape the next phase of the Gaza truce and Israel's role in the Iran war. My read: a long period of coalition bargaining, or even another election, looks more likely than a quick result.
topics.differences: Party-by-party seat counts differ slightly between outlets, for example for the Joint List and Ra'am, though all agree on the bloc totals of 53, 48 and 19[^15][^16].

question.text: Big Tech is borrowing and spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI data centres. If investors force these companies to slow down, who besides the companies themselves would feel it first, and how?

read.title: Alphabet's worst day ever leaves Google search valued below fossil fuel stocks, BofA says
read.summary: Why one quarter of heavy AI spending and slightly slower search growth wiped nearly $500 billion off Alphabet. A good primer on cash flow, valuations and what investors want from AI.
